1:
Barnes explains the force of the first epithet from the animals themselves, since dogs in the east are mostly masterless, wandering the streets and feeding on offal and even on corpses, held unclean, so that to call a man a dog is a far stronger contempt there than with us; and he notes the word came to mean a person shameless, impudent, snarling and contentious. Clarke and Robertson both observe the reversal at work, that this was the Jews' own name for the Gentiles, who stood outside the covenant, and that Paul now turns it on the Judaizing teachers themselves. Ellicott qualifies the reversal carefully: elsewhere the word marks the impure, and the party attacked here claimed a special purity and were probably not impure at all, the opposite fault belonging rather to the Antinomians censured at the end of the chapter; he credits Chrysostom with the hint that the name is retorted because by their wilful apostasy they now occupy the place outside the spiritual Israel that once belonged to the despised Gentiles. Robertson notes the warning is given three times over, with a different epithet each time.

The third epithet is a coinage and everyone stops on it. Clarke renders it the cutting or excision, deliberately not the word for circumcision, and takes it as degrading the pretension to sanctity that the Jews made by cutting their flesh: circumcision was honourable while it was the sign of the covenant, but having rejected the new covenant their cutting is reduced to mere mutilation. Robertson calls the noun a late word for incision or mutilation set against the ordinary word for circumcision, attested in one Greek version and an inscription, and notes that the related verb appears in the Greek Old Testament only of mutilations, in the law forbidding priests to cut themselves and in the account of the prophets of Baal. Gill, working from the Jewish side, reports that the name of dog which the Jews used for Gentiles is here returned upon them, and thinks they should not find the severity strange given what their own sources say. Barnes suggests the whole phrase may derive from the custom of posting a caution on a house guarded by a dog.

The claim that follows transfers the name rather than abolishing it. Calvin reads it as asserting that these are the true seed of Abraham and heirs of the covenant the sign confirmed, since the real circumcision is inward and seated in the heart rather than visible in the flesh; and he supplies the antithesis Paul leaves implicit, that the false apostles pressed an outward worship and boasted of being God's people because they kept the ceremonies. Ellicott gathers the Old Testament ground for the transfer, the command to circumcise the foreskin of the heart and the promise that the Lord will circumcise it, behind which lies the reproach of being uncircumcised in heart and ears. He also corrects the rendering, since the true reading is that we worship by the Spirit of God, and notes that the verb is the one almost technically used of Israel's worship as God's chosen people. Robertson allows three constructions of the same phrase and finds good sense in each. Gill describes the inward circumcision in stages, the heart pricked, its hardness removed, its iniquity laid open. Barnes states the design of the rite as emblematic from the first.
4:
The list of credentials is read as an argument rather than a boast, and the commentators work through it item by item. Robertson catches the logic of the opening, that Paul claims more ground for confidence than his opponents and then proves it in what follows. On the first item all agree that the eighth day marks a Jew born rather than a proselyte, Robertson noting that Ishmaelites were circumcised in the thirteenth year and Gentile proselytes at mature age; Clarke adds that the law required it and that both the Samaritan Pentateuch and the Greek version preserve a clause, now lost from the common Hebrew text, cutting off the child not circumcised on that day. Ellicott takes the tribe as pointedly chosen, being the tribe of the first king whose name the apostle bore, the tribe to which the holy city belonged, and the one that stayed faithful when the rest fell away; Clarke makes the same point about its not revolting with Jeroboam nor polluting the worship of God with idols. On the last item Ellicott explains that a Hebrew descended from Hebrews kept the old tongue and customs wherever born, and held himself superior to the Hellenist.

Barnes reads the whole catalogue as a claim about salvation rather than about pedigree, since these were the things Paul had valued as of vast advantage in that matter and had supposed made him rich in religion; he adds that they also opened a brilliant prospect of honour and office, commending him to the rulers of the nation and making advancement certain. Calvin insists on the exactness rather than the fact of the rite, that the circumcision was performed duly and according to the appointment of the law, and that such customary circumcision was reckoned of superior value besides being a token of race, foreigners being circumcised in youth or manhood or sometimes in old age. Robertson puts the accounting metaphor plainly, that these were gains on the credit side of the ledger, and that Paul had a natural pride in them, having been the star of hope for Gamaliel and the Sanhedrin. Clarke describes what was lost by the change, the credit and respect he had enjoyed as one zealously attached to the law and the traditions of the elders, and what he came to see, that no act of righteousness could be depended on for salvation.

On the reversal itself the readings diverge in a way worth marking. Ellicott presses the phrase harder than the others, taking the loss as not merely worthless but worse than worthless, because such privilege prevents the sense of spiritual need and helplessness that should bring a man to Christ, so that in gaining all the world he tends to the loss of his own soul. Calvin locates the cause rather than the effect, holding that ignorance of Christ is the sole reason we are puffed up with a vain confidence, so that where a false estimate of one's own excellence appears, there Christ is not known; the moment Christ shines forth, whatever had dazzled the eyes with a false splendour vanishes or is at least disesteemed. His sharpest word is that nothing was so injurious to Paul as his own righteousness, since we are not received by Christ except as naked and emptied of it. Chrysostom reports that the heretics of his day seized on this very verse, arguing that if Paul calls the law loss and refuse it cannot be of God, and that the apostle let them take the bait before enclosing them with his nets.
8:
Two figures dominate the eighth verse. Barnes and Calvin both reach independently for seamen: Barnes has Paul regard his gains as sailors do the goods on which they set a high value, willing to throw them all overboard to save themselves, while Calvin presses the same similitude further and then withdraws part of it, since men who jettison cargo part with it regretfully and bewail the loss once ashore, whereas Paul held his gains offensive. The second figure is the word rendered dung. Robertson calls it a late word of uncertain etymology, either connected with a term for dung or from a phrase meaning to fling to the dogs, occurring here only in the New Testament and found in the papyri. Ellicott, citing Lightfoot for instances of its use for the fragments of a feast, notes that the old derivation from what is thrown to dogs, however etymologically questionable, would suit the retort of that name upon the Judaisers earlier in the chapter. Wesley marks the escalation: loss is sustained with patience, but dung is cast away with abhorrence. Robertson counts five particles stacked before the sentence begins, showing the force and passion of the conviction.

The ninth verse produces a genuine disagreement over a single verb. Calvin declines the passive that everyone else adopts, arguing that the Greek, though passive in termination, carries an active signification meaning to recover what you have voluntarily given up, so that Paul renounced everything in order to recover it in Christ; and he adds the proverb that he had been lost if he had not been lost. Gill notes the divergence explicitly, allows that Calvin's sense is true in substance since carnal privileges are exchanged for spiritual blessings and one's own righteousness for a better, yet judges it best to read the words passively. Henry supplies the image the others leave implicit, that to be found in him is to be found as the manslayer was found in the city of refuge, safe from the avenger of blood, or else as a man is found of his Judge in peace. On the two righteousnesses Calvin and Ellicott converge from different angles. Calvin insists the one must be renounced entirely for the other, since the law brings works while faith presents man naked before God. Ellicott reads the verse as defining faith first as means and then, more exactly, as the sole condition of a gift originating with God.

Barnes takes the fellowship of the sufferings as the hard clause and presses it as a test: many are willing to reign with Christ but not to suffer with him, willing to wear the crown of glory but not the crown of thorns, willing to put on the robes of splendour but not the scarlet robe of mockery. Calvin distinguishes two participations in that death, the inward mortification of the flesh treated in the sixth chapter of Romans and the outward endurance of the cross treated in the eighth, and holds that our whole life must represent nothing but the image of death until it produce death itself. Clarke narrows the fellowship differently, observing that no creature can share the vicarious sufferings and that Paul wished to imitate Christ as a martyr to the truth. On the last verse Clarke, Robertson and Gill all rest on the compound noun the apostle uses here and nowhere else, reading it as the resurrection out from among the dead rather than the general rising; Robertson adds that this is no denial of a general resurrection, and Gill that everyone will attain to that one, Pharaoh and Judas included. The opening qualification, Robertson and Gill agree, expresses humility rather than doubt.
12:
The denial of having been already perfected sets the commentators against each other more sharply than anything else in the chapter. Barnes takes it as moral, a distinct assertion that Paul did not regard himself as free from sin, and asks who could urge better claims to perfection than he, concluding that whoever claims a holiness Paul did not pretend to shows little true knowledge of himself; he notes honestly that many critics, Clarke among them, refer the word instead to the games. Clarke is that party, and holds the point emphatically: the verb is used of those who have completed their race and are honoured with the prize, and it had come to mean martyrdom outright, which he documents from Philo, from Clement of Alexandria defining it as the consummation of the work of charity rather than the end of life, from Basil, Oecumenius and Eusebius. On that reading Paul speaks of no deficiency in his own grace, and the contrary opinion Clarke calls most falsely and dangerously imagined. Robertson and Ellicott sit nearer Barnes without his heat, Robertson saying Paul knew nothing of absolute perfection by a single experience, Ellicott that attaining is one act and being perfected a continuous process.

Underneath the dispute all of them agree that the whole passage is built on the Grecian foot-race, Clarke marking one continued allusion running from the eleventh verse to the seventeenth and reminding us that the Philippians knew the contests and their laws well. Calvin unfolds the similitude into three requirements: that it profits the runner nothing to have left the starting-point unless he goes forward to the goal, so we must pursue our calling until death; that the way is marked out so that he need not tire himself wandering in this direction or that; and that he must be free from entanglement, surmounting every obstacle rather than stopping at it. Ellicott observes that Paul then breaks his own metaphor. Unwilling to rest too much weight on his exertions, he interrupts the picture of the eager runner stretching to grasp the prize with the remembrance that he was himself once grasped, at his conversion, by the hand of Christ, and so only put in a condition to grasp anything; the hope of apprehending rests on having been apprehended by one out of whose hand no man can pluck him. Calvin puts the same thought more briefly, that Paul did nothing except under Christ's influence and guidance.

On forgetting what lies behind, Chrysostom is the most exact reader: the runner reckons not how many circuits he has finished but how many are left, and Paul did not say that he declines to reckon them up but that he does not even remember; the man who thinks all accomplished may cease running, while he who thinks himself still distant from the goal never will. Of the stretching forward he says the runner endeavours to outstrip his own feet, throwing his body toward the front and reaching out his hands to gain a little more of the course. Calvin raises the obvious objection, that recalling past mercies encourages hope and past sins prompt amendment, and answers that such thoughts do not turn the view backward but help the sight of the goal; what Paul condemns is only the looking back that destroys alacrity. Ellicott makes the precept absolutely general, covering past blessings, past achievements and even past sins. On the mark itself Clarke keeps to the stadium, taking it for the white line from start to goal which a runner who strayed beyond was not crowned for crossing first, while Gill and Robertson both make it Christ himself, the goal on which the eye stays fixed.
15:
Having just denied that he was perfected, the apostle addresses the perfect four verses later, and the commentators divide over the tone. Gill and Ellicott both allow that the word may be ironical, Gill adding the alternative that it is comparative rather than absolute and concerns parts rather than degrees; Ellicott thinks the irony aimed at those who held themselves already to have attained, and draws out the paradox that Paul bids such men prove their perfection by a consciousness of imperfection, so that if they lack it they have something yet to learn. Robertson takes the plainer road, that the term here means relative perfection and that Paul includes himself among the spiritual adults, in contrast to the absolute perfection so pointedly denied above. Clarke fills in the usage from elsewhere, where the word marks those who are grown men rather than children in understanding, adults in Christian knowledge, thoroughly instructed and experienced. Barnes hesitates over the address itself and prefers to read it as those who would be perfect or are aiming at it, since it can hardly be supposed that Paul would call them what he had just refused to call himself. Wesley glosses it briefly as fit for the race.

The promise that God will reveal even this is read by everyone as forbearance rather than concession. Robertson puts it most bluntly, that Paul turns such cases over to God, asking what else he could do with them. Calvin makes the sentence do double work, humbling the readers and giving them good hope at once: they are admonished not to be elated in their ignorance and at the same time told to take courage, since a man must make way for the revelation of God if he has not yet attained what he seeks, and obstinacy is the great obstacle to truth, so that the best preparation for docility is not to take pleasure in error. He then draws the pastoral inference that we must bear for a time with ignorance in weaker brethren and forgive them if it is not given them at once to be of one mind with us, observing that Paul was entirely assured of his own doctrine yet allowed those who could not receive it time to make progress and did not on that account cease to treat them as brethren. Clarke and Barnes both attach the promise to sincerity, Barnes taking it as an assurance that true Christians will be led on until they understand.

The sixteenth verse carries a textual problem that four of the commentators raise independently. Clarke reports that the manuscripts, versions and fathers of the Alexandrian text omit the words rendered by the same rule and mind the same thing, that the disagreement among copies is wide enough for most critics to treat them as a gloss never original to the text, and that one editor pronounced them most certainly to be deleted. Ellicott agrees the closing words are an explanatory gloss, partly borrowed from the end of Galatians, and gives the original as a bare instruction to walk by whatever we did attain; Robertson notes the same absence of the word for rule in the oldest witnesses; Calvin observes that the Greek copies differ even over where to divide the clauses. What survives the excision is a rule of forbearance, and Barnes and Henry both build on it. Henry has believers who differ over meats and days refrain from judging one another because they meet in Christ as their centre and hope to meet in heaven as their home. Barnes turns it into a working maxim for church quarrels, that where we cannot yet agree we should agree to differ, labouring together at what we hold in common.
17:
The call to imitation is guarded on every side. Ellicott notes that the word is peculiar, signifying not simply follow me but unite in following me, so that the example serves unity as well as rectitude; Robertson renders it with Lightfoot as a summons to vie with each other in imitating him, and observes that the verb for marking others means to keep the eyes on them as a goal, here to follow rather than to avoid. Calvin removes the suspicion of ambition from it, remarking that Paul does not care whom they single out provided they conform to the purity of which he was a pattern, since a man devoted to his own interests wishes no rival. Gill guards it from the other direction, that Paul never assumed a dominion over the faith of men and asked to be followed no further than he followed Christ. Clarke, still inside the stadium, has him say that his writings, preaching and conduct are to be their line. Of the tears that follow, Henry observes that Paul was on occasion a weeping preacher as Jeremiah was a weeping prophet, and that an old sermon may be preached with new affections; Calvin takes them as evidence that no envy or hatred moved him.

Who the enemies of the cross are is genuinely disputed. Clarke identifies them flatly as the Judaizing teachers, who attribute justification to the Levitical sacrifices rather than to the death of Christ, please the world and are in no danger of reproach. Chrysostom sees the opposite fault, men who made a pretence of Christianity yet lived in ease and luxury: thy Master was crucified, and dost thou seek ease; thy Master was pierced with nails, and dost thou live delicately; did they love the cross they would strive to live the crucified life. Ellicott takes them for an Antinomian party sheltering its profligacy under Paul's own preaching of liberty, and adds that the doctrine of the cross has two parts, the one Christ alone bore and we can only believe, the other we are to take up and follow him in, so that men accepting the first may be enemies of the second. Robertson offers both identifications as open alternatives. Calvin canvasses the explanations of others and settles on a general reading, that these were not open adversaries but impostors who trampled the power of the gospel for the sake of ambition or of their own belly, and did more injury than if they had opposed Christ outright.

Against those who mind earthly things stands a word found nowhere else in the New Testament. Barnes explains that it does not mean conversation in our modern sense but the administration of a state, and then the community itself, so that the verse sets two societies against each other, one governed by worldly laws and one by the laws of heaven. Clarke reaches the same conclusion from the lexicons. Ellicott weighs the grammar and prefers our city to our citizenship, and draws the point home to the readers: as the inhabitants of a Roman colony were citizens of a far distant imperial city, so these Philippians were already citizens of the better country. Robertson reports Milligan's doubt whether the colony rendering is defensible at all, since it reverses the relation between colony and mother city. On the closing promise Ellicott corrects the familiar rendering, insisting the body is not really vile but is the body of our humiliation, and that humiliation is only its outward fashion; Gill anticipates the same distinction, that the change is in qualities and not in substance or form. Calvin measures the glory by the transfiguration, asking who could bear its fullness when the disciples could not endure the slight taste afforded there.
